title: Common Misperceptions Regarding Moments of Genuine Connection
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart addresses three misconceptions that commonly arise once teachers begin tracking Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs), his framework for building relational Credibility with students. First, he cautions against treating MGCs as a uniform checklist item imposed from outside, arguing that genuine connection requires teachers to find rhythms and language that feel authentic to their own personality and classroom routines. Second, he stresses that MGC content matters: attempts should be roughly balanced between personal and academic topics so students perceive teachers as caring about them holistically, not just performing niceness. Third, he normalizes the reality that MGCs are not always easy or pleasant, some attempts will be awkward or land flat, and that difficulty doesn't mean the practice has failed. The piece functions as a troubleshooting guide for schools or teachers rolling out MGC tracking as a schoolwide initiative.
points: MGCs lose their power when reduced to a uniform, externally mandated checklist; genuine connection requires teacher-specific rhythms and authentic language.
Effective MGCs need rough balance between personal and academic content so students perceive holistic Care, one leg of the Credibility framework.
Stuart explicitly normalizes MGC attempts that feel awkward or fall flat, reframing difficulty as expected rather than a sign of doing it wrong.
The piece serves as a practical troubleshooting guide for schools rolling out relationship-building practices at scale, where fidelity concerns often creep in.
quotes: Once folks start trying to implement tracking attempted moments of genuine connection (MGCs), there are a few misperceptions that start to crop up.
If MGC attempts become some "got-to-do-it" thing that external forces are pushing onto our plates, it's pretty likely that we'll end up missing the G in MGC. They won't be genuine.

To fix this, you've got to find rhythms and routines that make MGCs make sense to you. Maybe all of your MGC attempts are during class passing times; maybe they are all during an independent work portion of your lesson.

For MGC attempts to have their best effects on the Credibility belief, they need to be roughly balanced into both personal and academic categories. We want to send signals that indicate our Care, holistically, for each of our students.

While lots of MGC attempts are going to give you the warm fuzzies and feel pretty effortless, it's unreasonable to expect that you'll have an easy time connecting with all of your students. Sometimes these are awkward.
